summary: Explains how IKEv1, IKEv2, and IPsec use hash functions and how vulnerable these protocols are to the reduced collision resistance of MD5 and SHA-1. It helps readers judge the practical impact of weaknesses found in those hashes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some secret-stamp tools have cracks. This note checks where Internet security systems use those tools and whether the cracks actually let anyone in.

subtitle: How hash algorithm weaknesses affect IPsec and IKE security.

tldr.problem: Attacks on the collision-resistance of MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions have been discovered, raising questions about whether these protocols remain secure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews exactly how IKEv1, IKEv2, and IPsec use hash functions and concludes that neither IKE nor IPsec are susceptible to the known collision-reduction attacks on these hashes.
tldr.outcome: IKE and IPsec do not need protocol changes. Implementors should strongly consider supporting SHA-2 family algorithms and alternatives like AES-XCBC, but MD5 and SHA-1 need not be prohibited.

today: RFC 4894 remains relevant as a reference for understanding how hash algorithms are deployed in IKE and IPsec. While MD5 and SHA-1 are considered deprecated for new applications, this RFC explained why existing deployments need not rush to disable them. Modern implementations should prioritize SHA-2 family algorithms and AES-based alternatives.

sections.title: Overview of Hash Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
Recent cryptanalytic research discovered attacks on the collision-resistance properties of MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions. A collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash output; collision-resistance attacks aim to find two messages with the same hash more efficiently than brute-force methods.

The security community began examining all Internet protocols to determine whether they rely on collision-resistance and whether known attacks pose practical threats. This document reviews three critical protocols: IKEv1 (Phase 1 and agreement process), IKEv2 (IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH exchanges), and IPsec (Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload). The analysis concludes that despite being widely used with MD5 and SHA-1, none of these protocols are susceptible to practical collision-reduction attacks.
sections.eli5: Researchers found ways to trick MD5 and SHA-1 into producing the same result for different inputs. People got worried that this would break Internet security. This document checks three big security protocols to see if they actually break. Spoiler: they don't.

sections.title: How IKE Uses Hash Functions
sections.content:
IKEv1 and IKEv2 use hash functions as pseudo-random functions (PRFs) to derive keys. Critically, the inputs to these PRFs include nonce values generated by both the initiator and responder that neither party can predict. IKEv1 nonces are at least 64 bits; IKEv2 nonces are at least 128 bits. Because of this unpredictability, the use of hashes as PRFs is not susceptible to collision-reduction attacks: an attacker cannot create two messages with the same hash when both messages depend on a nonce they did not predict.

IKEv2 also uses hashes in Hashed Message Authentication Codes (HMACs) for integrity protection of messages after the initial exchange. Research shows MD5 in HMAC can be forged and SHA-1 suspected of being forgeable, but there is no known practical reason for an attacker to forge a legitimate message—only the IKE entity creating the message wants it to be authentic.

Both versions support digital signatures for authentication. An attacker who finds a collision could theoretically create two certificates with different identities but the same signature hash. However, the attacker must be the certificate holder to compute valid signatures on both messages, making this attack of limited practical value.
sections.eli5: IKE uses hash functions to mix secret numbers together. Because the secret numbers include unpredictable surprises from both sides, even a broken hash function cannot fool the system. HMAC forgery is theoretically possible but nobody would actually use it this way.

sections.title: How IPsec Uses Hash Functions
sections.content:
IPsec uses hashes exclusively in HMACs for authenticating packets in both the Authentication Header (AH) and the optional authentication function of Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). Like IKEv2 HMACs, IPsec HMACs are used for packet authentication, where only the legitimate sender would want to create authentic packets.

Research shows that MD5 and SHA-1 used in HMACs are susceptible to forgery attacks in theory, but practical exploitation is extremely unlikely. The attacker would need to forge a packet authentication code to change network traffic undetected, but they would have no incentive to produce a forgery that appears to come from a legitimate peer. The IPsec SPI (Security Parameter Index) and sequence numbering provide additional protection against out-of-order or replay attacks.
sections.eli5: IPsec uses hashes to sign every packet, like putting a wax seal on it. Breaking the wax seal process doesn't help an attacker much, because they would need to forge a legitimate seal, and nobody would trust a seal they forged themselves.

sections.title: Choosing and Negotiating Cryptographic Functions
sections.content:
IKEv1, IKEv2, and IPsec all allow negotiation of different hash functions for every place where collision-resistance matters. This protocol flexibility means that as new attacks emerge or preferred algorithms change, implementations can deploy stronger functions without protocol changes.

When protocols allow multiple functions, the initiator (the "proposer") lists all functions it supports, and the responder (the "chooser") selects one. The RFC discusses whether the chooser should be able to signal back additional functions the proposer didn't offer. Current IKE implementations do not support this signaling, but the presence of protocol flexibility means this is not a limiting factor.

For public key certificates used in IKE authentication, the situation is different. Certificate signers (certification authorities) control which hash functions are used, so IKE implementors cannot unilaterally change the hash algorithms in certificates. However, both IKEv1 and IKEv2 allow multiple certificates to be presented, giving each party options.
sections.eli5: These protocols let you pick which hash function to use from a list. If one gets broken, you switch to another without rewriting the protocol. That is good design.

sections.title: Guidance for Protocol Designers and Implementors
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that IKEv1 and IKEv2 do not require protocol changes to remain secure against known hash attacks. Both protocols already allow agreement on hash functions, and both allow multiple certificates for authentication. No changes are needed to the core protocols.

However, implementors are strongly encouraged to add support for alternatives, particularly AES-XCBC-PRF-128 for pseudo-random functions and AES-XCBC-MAC-96 for message authentication, as well as the SHA-2 family (SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512) for HMAC. Implementors of IKE that use PKIX certificate authentication should strongly consider supporting certificates signed with SHA-2 algorithms and enabling multiple certificate support. These additions future-proof implementations against potential weaknesses in older algorithms while maintaining backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: IKE and IPsec are fine as they are. But implementors should add support for newer, stronger hash functions so they can upgrade when they want to.
